::: {.lead}
Today you fact-check a short text that an AI wrote, from the first claim to
the corrected text. Each experiment has two parts. **Part A** is in Word
and a search engine on the lab computer. **Part B** is on a simulator of
the interactive lesson: on paper, scan its QR code; on the screen, click
its link. After each step, write your result in its box. At the end, copy
your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a lab computer with Word and a browser with a search engine
  (`bing.com`).
- **No lab computer today?** Do Part B of each experiment on your phone. Do
  Part A later on any computer with Word.
- **The AI-written text** for the staff newsletter of Sunrise Company (it
  is also on the interactive lesson, to copy):

  > **Walk more at work!** The World Health Organization says that adults
  > should be active for at least 150 minutes a week. A study by Omar
  > Haddad (Journal of Office Steps, 2020) showed that workers who walk
  > 10,000 steps a day make 50 % fewer mistakes. Walking uses no energy at
  > all. Every good manager knows that his staff walk too little. Walking
  > is always better than every other sport.

- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

## Experiment 1 · Find every claim

**The idea:** a **claim** can be checked: a number, a date, a name, a price,
a quote, "a study shows", "experts say". An opinion ("walking is fun") is
not a claim. Highlight every claim before you check anything.

**Aim:** find the claims of the text.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Word)**
:::

1. Copy the AI-written text into a new Word document. Highlight every claim
   in yellow (**Home › Text Highlight Color**).

   {{< record "The claims: … (how many?)" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Five claims**: 150 minutes a week (the WHO); the study by Omar Haddad
   with 50 % fewer mistakes; walking uses no energy; every good manager
   knows that his staff walk too little; walking is always better than
   every other sport. The title is not a claim.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   A claim to check, or not a claim? Sort the parts of the text.

   A claim: check it
   :   The World Health Organization says: at least 150 minutes a week.

       Why: A number and a source: it can be checked.

   :   A study by Omar Haddad (2020) showed 50 % fewer mistakes.

       Why: A study, a year and a number: check them.

   :   Walking uses no energy at all.

       Why: A fact that can be checked.

   Not a claim
   :   Walk more at work!

       Why: A title that asks something; nothing to check.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-11/sims/claim-finder.html" poster="../../week-11/sims/claim-finder.png" title="Claim Finder: which sentences can be checked?" >}}

2. In **Claim Finder**, mark the sentences about tea that can be checked.
   Which sentences are opinions?

   {{< record "The opinions: …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Three opinions**: "Green tea is the best drink for the morning", "Tea
   tastes better with fresh mint" and "A warm cup on a cold evening is a
   lovely thing". The other five sentences are claims: a number, a study,
   a date, "experts say" and a price.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   "Experts say that three cups a day are enough." What is it?

   - [x] a claim: which experts? check it

     Why: "Experts say" must be checked like a source.

   - [ ] an opinion

     Why: It is said as a fact by experts, so it can be checked.

   - [ ] a title

     Why: It is a full sentence with a fact.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · Check facts and sources

**The idea:** check each claim in **two reliable sources**: official health
organisations, universities, encyclopedias, known newspapers. Open other
pages about the claim (**lateral reading**). For a study, search the
title, the authors and the journal. Then decide: **keep**, **correct**
(with the source) or **remove**.

**Aim:** check two claims of the text, and decide what to do.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (a search engine)**
:::

1. Check two claims. First the WHO claim: search *WHO physical activity
   adults* and open the page of the World Health Organization and one more
   reliable page. Then the study: search *Omar Haddad Journal of Office
   Steps 2020*.

   {{< record "150 minutes: … ; the study: … ; my actions: …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **150 minutes:** true; the WHO page says at least 150 minutes of
   activity a week for adults: **keep**. **The study:** no search finds the
   author, the journal or the study: a made-up source: **remove**.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   No search finds the study, its author or its journal. What do you do?

   - [x] Remove the claim: it is a made-up source.

     Why: A study that no search finds does not exist.

   - [ ] Keep it: the numbers look exact.

     Why: Exact numbers can be invented too.

   - [ ] Ask the same AI if the study is real.

     Why: The AI that invented it is not a source.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-11/sims/claim-court.html" poster="../../week-11/sims/claim-court.png" title="Claim Court: judge the AI answers" kind="game" >}}

2. Play **Claim Court**: colleagues bring six AI answers; choose the
   judgement and the action. What is your judgement of the AI table with
   Paper 75 + Drinks 50 + Bags 60 = 195 JD?

   {{< record "The table: …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **A wrong sum: compute it yourself**: 75 + 50 + 60 = 185 JD, not 195.
   AI can make mistakes with numbers.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="185" unit="JD" hint="75 + 50 + 60."}
   The AI table says Paper 75 + Drinks 50 + Bags 60 = 195 JD. What is the
   right total?

   Why: 75 + 50 + 60 = 185 JD. Compute a sum yourself; do not trust the AI's number.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · Fair words and a check log

**The idea:** look for **stereotypes** and one-sided parts, and rewrite them
with neutral words and both sides. Keep a **check log**, a table with four
columns: claim · source · result · action. End the corrected text with an
**AI-use statement**: what the AI did, and that you checked it.

**Aim:** write the check log and a fair corrected text.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Word)**
:::

1. Under the text, insert a table with **4 columns** (Insert › Table):
   *Claim*, *Source*, *Result*, *Action*. Fill in one row for each of the
   three claims about walking, the study and the energy.

   {{< record "My row for the study: …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   For example: *A study by Omar Haddad (2020)* · *searches of the title,
   the author and the journal* · *made up* · *remove*. And: *Walking uses
   no energy* · *a health organisation page* · *wrong* · *correct: walking
   uses energy*.
   :::

   ::: {.order}
   Put the columns of a check log in order.

   1. Claim
   2. Source
   3. Result
   4. Action

   Why: What the AI said, where you checked it, what you found, and what you do.
   :::

2. Write the corrected text under the table: keep the true claims, correct
   the wrong one, remove the made-up study, and rewrite the two unfair
   sentences. End with: *Draft written with AI help and checked by …*
   (your name).

   {{< record "My fair sentence for the manager … ; my last sentence …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   For example: "Many people at work walk too little" (neutral, no "his"),
   and "Walking is one good way to stay active; other sports help too"
   (both sides). The last sentence says what the AI did and that you
   checked it.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   "Walking is always better than every other sport." What do you do?

   - [x] Give both sides: walking is one good way; other sports help too.

     Why: A one-sided claim needs both sides with reasons.

   - [ ] Keep it: it says something good.

     Why: "Always better" is one-sided and not true.

   - [ ] Write it in capital letters.

     Why: The look does not make it fair.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-11/sims/bias-lab.html" poster="../../week-11/sims/bias-lab.png" title="Bias Lab: who does the AI show, and how?" >}}

3. In **Bias Lab**, do the three requests and add the instruction that
   removes the red parts. Which instruction fits "Working from home is
   always better"?

   {{< record "Working from home: …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Give both sides with reasons**: a one-sided text needs the good and
   the bad sides. The doctor and the nurse need neutral language.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   "Every office manager knows her team." What do you do?

   - [x] Use neutral language: "Every office manager knows the team."

     Why: The job is not only for women.

   - [ ] Keep it: it is polite.

     Why: Polite words can still hold a stereotype.

   - [ ] Delete the whole text.

     Why: Change the unfair words; the rest can stay.
   :::
